items.text: If you've rested through burnout and returned to the same demands, the same masking requirements, the same environment — that's not recovery. That's a pause before the next cycle.
items.rationale: Directly names why rest alone fails autistic people in burnout. Reframes relapse as a predictable system outcome rather than individual failure. The parallel structure ('same demands, same masking, same environment') earns the landing.

items.text: Rest doesn't cure autistic burnout. It pauses it. Recovery means changing what you return to — not just building the stamina to face it again.
items.rationale: Strips the burnout-rest relationship to its plainest form and pivots to the actionable implication: structural change, not endurance. Different angle from post 1 — this is the prescription, not the diagnosis.

items.text: It was never the last straw. It was every straw, for thirty years, arriving together on the same statement. That's what late-diagnosed autistic burnout actually looks like.
items.rationale: The bank-statement metaphor explains the seemingly disproportionate collapse — why something small can finally break a person who 'seemed fine for decades.' Late-diagnosed readers will recognize this immediately.

items.text: Most late-diagnosed autistic people spent decades masking without knowing they were spending anything. By the time the balance was checked, the account was empty.
items.rationale: 'Most' qualifier avoids speaking for all. The expenditure metaphor is vivid without being clinical. Validates the late-diagnosis experience — the collapse feels sudden because no one knew to track the deficit.

items.text: When the demand hits, the thinking brain doesn't slow down — it goes offline. That's not defiance. That's the PDA profile.
items.rationale: Gives PDA individuals and their families a neurologically grounded reframe for a behaviour constantly misread as wilful opposition. Short and confident — built to be screenshot and shared with someone who needs to hear it.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Thinking brain goes offline' is a simplification of the amygdala-prefrontal mechanism described in the source. Defensible as an approximation, but not a clinical claim — framed correctly as profile description, not diagnosis.

items.text: Low-demand parenting doesn't mean no demands. It means being deliberate about which demands are worth the cost — and letting go of the ones that aren't.
items.rationale: Names the specific conflation that derails families and provides the corrective in a single sentence. Practical and discussion-generating without shaming anyone on either side of the debate.

items.text: Low-demand parenting and zero-demand parenting aren't the same thing. Treating them as identical is exactly why the approach fails — and why families get blamed for it.
items.rationale: Shifts blame for approach failure from families onto the conceptual confusion. Distinct from post 6: this is the structural critique, not the definition. Relevant to the March 2026 discourse actively circulating.

items.text: Remote work accidentally became the most effective workplace accommodation many autistic people ever had. Nobody designed it that way. Is undoing it with an RTO mandate a neutral business decision?
items.rationale: Reframes the RTO debate from productivity to access. The 'nobody designed it' line names a structural irony; the question forces a genuine reckoning without being agitprop. Timely — May 2026 HR discourse is live.

items.text: Having to choose between disclosing your neurodivergence or losing a work setup that actually functions isn't a personal problem to solve. That's a structural one.
items.rationale: Validates the specific RTO bind without prescribing disclosure. Moves responsibility from individual to system. Uses 'neurodivergence' deliberately — broader than autism, relevant to more readers facing this exact situation.

items.text: Getting a late diagnosis doesn't always quiet the inner voice. Sometimes the first thing it says is: 'but surely you're not as autistic as a real autistic person.'
items.rationale: Names post-diagnosis imposter syndrome by quoting the internalized thought itself — so readers feel seen rather than lectured. The harmful phrase is framed as 'the inner voice,' not as a statement of fact.
items.sensitivity_flag: Deliberately quotes an internalized ableist thought to name and validate the experience. Could be misread stripped of context — 'the inner voice' framing is the guardrail. Low risk; worth monitoring how it lands in replies.

items.text: For AuDHD people, demand avoidance doesn't only fire when someone else makes a request. Your own to-do list can trigger the same alarm. 'Just start' can make it worse.
items.rationale: Articulates something AuDHD people experience constantly but rarely see named: self-directed demands firing the same avoidance response as external ones. The practical implication is embedded without moralizing.

items.text: For autistic adults whose burnout cycles are getting shorter: what actually changed? Research suggests the common thread is self-knowledge — not a new treatment or medication.
items.rationale: Opens a genuine discussion prompt anchored in a research-backed finding. The question invites personal responses; 'Research suggests' hedges appropriately without diluting the insight. Hopeful without being cure-framed.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Not a new treatment or medication' reflects source data accurately but could be misread as dismissing professional support. Phrasing is comparative, not prescriptive — not medical advice. Low risk; worth ensuring the post stands alone without anti-treatment readings.
